name: Fire Island National Seashore
author: parks-page-legacy
summary: Fire Island National Seashore, established in 1964, protects a 26-mile stretch of barrier island off the southern shore of Long Island, New York — one of the last remaining undeveloped barrier beaches on the Atlantic Coast. The national seashore was created after a fierce conservation battle to prevent large-scale resort development on the island. The park includes the Sunken Forest, a rare 300-year-old maritime holly forest growing behind the dunes, and the Fire Island Lighthouse, first constructed in 1826 and rebuilt in 1858. The William Floyd Estate, the ancestral home of a signer of the Declaration of Independence, is also part of the seashore. Fire Island has historically served as a significant cultural refuge for LGBTQ communities, particularly the communities of Cherry Grove and Fire Island Pines.
